title: Hypothesis Tests & A/B Testing
summary: Turn a conversion-rate experiment into a decision. Learn the pooled two-proportion z-test and its two-sided p-value, the unpooled interval for the lift, how to size a test from a minimum detectable effect, and why a sample-ratio-mismatch check has to come before reading any metric.
takeaways: The z-test pools both arms because H0 says they share one rate. The lift's confidence interval uses the unpooled SE.
Report two-sided p-values: p = 2·(1 − Φ(|z|)). A p-value is not an effect size, so always show the interval too.
Fix the sample size up front from baseline, MDE, α and power. Halving the MDE roughly quadruples n.
A sample ratio mismatch makes the experiment untrustworthy. Check it first and don't read the metric if it fires.

steps.label: Plan
steps.detail: Choose α, power and the minimum detectable effect, and compute users per arm.

steps.label: Run to n
steps.detail: Collect data until the planned sample size, without stopping on a lucky p-value.

steps.label: SRM check
steps.detail: Chi-square test of observed vs designed split. If it fails, stop and debug.

steps.label: Test
steps.detail: Pooled two-proportion z-test with a two-sided p-value.

steps.label: Estimate
steps.detail: Confidence interval for the lift with the unpooled SE.

terms.definition: The default claim being tested. In an A/B test, that both arms have the same true rate.
The probability, assuming H0, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed.
SE computed from the combined rate of both arms, valid under H0, used for the test statistic.
The probability of detecting a true effect of a given size, usually set to 80%.
The smallest true change the test is designed to detect at the chosen α and power.
When the observed split of users across arms differs significantly from the designed split, signalling a broken experiment.
